newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Vatican welcomes Yeltsin veto on religion bill.
newsitem.headline: Vatican welcomes Yeltsin veto on religion bill.

text.p: Roman Catholics and human rights activists on Wednesday welcomed Boris Yeltsin's rejection of a draft law curbing religious freedom in Russia while his communist opponents pledged to fight the presidential veto.
There was a confused silence from the powerful Orthodox Church, which had stood to benefit from the law in this latest battle for Russians' souls.
Yeltsin, under pressure from the Vatican and the United States, blocked the law late on Tuesday on the grounds that it contradicted the Russian constitution.

The bill, approved by a majority of parliamentarians who said it would help clamp down on dangerous foreign sects, identified Orthodoxy, Islam, Buddhism and Judaism as traditional faiths in the multi-ethnic Russian Federation.

Representatives of other confessions, including Catholicism which has a long history of tension with the newly-resurgent Orthodox Church, fear that the vaguely-worded bill could result in them losing their legal rights.
Human Rights Watch/Helsinki praised Yeltsin's veto in a statement, saying the current draft used the threat posed by quasi-religious sects as a pretext to curb religious freedoms.
"We are very happy with the decision," activist Diederik Lohman said by telephone. "But we're not quite there yet," he added, noting that parliament could override the veto.

John Bukovsky, the Vatican's ambassador to Moscow, also welcomed Yeltsin's decision, which followed an appeal from Pope John Paul II. "The head of the Vatican considered this document undemocratic, limiting the freedom of religious and generally accepted world standards," Bukovsky said.
"We consider Catholicism a traditional religion with a 300-year history in Russia," he added, saying that Russia's 150 million population included a million practising Catholics.
Communists meanwhile rushed to the side of the Orthodox Church, in a sharp reversal of their predecessors' determined atheism which underlined their new, nationalist bent.

Prominent communist Viktor Iluykhin said Yeltsin's veto showed yet again that Russia had become a protectorate of the West, referring to and a threat by U.S. senators to withhold around $200 million worth of aid.
Ilyukhin's colleague Valentin Kuptsov took up the theme.

"One must be sorry that the president listened not to the views of senior clergymen of the Russian Orthodox Church but to voices from across the ocean," he said in comments published by Interfax news agency.

A spokeswoman for the Moscow Patriarchy said there would be no comment from the Church on the veto on Wednesday. Patriarch Alexiy II, who has hitherto enjoyed strong support from Yeltsin, was due to respond on Thursday.

Aware of the sensitivity of his decision in a country where sympathy for the Orthodox Church and fear of foreign sects run deep, Yeltsin took the highly unusual step of explaining his veto in an address to the nation.
"This was a difficult decision. The law was after all supported by 370 State Duma (lower house) deputies and 10 other basic religious organisations in Russia," he wrote.
Yeltsin said he had sent his proposals to parliament and appealed to deputies to amend the law.

But the extent of support for the bill among politicians keen to appeal to voters scared by many of the sects which flooded Russia after communism fell, means the issue is far from resolved. Deputies, due to reconvene in September, can override Yeltsin's veto with a two-thirds majority in both chambers.
